extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the key proof techniques, definitions, and methodological steps presented in textbook chapters on the cotangent/Herglotz trick, Buffon’s needle, and combinatorics (pigeon-hole and double counting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial fraction expansion of cotangent
rubrics_metrics.description: π cot πx = lim_{N→∞} Σ_{n=-N}^N 1/(x + n) (x ∈ R \ Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula is Euler's classical partial fraction expansion. Warning: the series is only conditionally convergent, so its value depends on the 'right' order of summation; care is required when evaluating or rearranging the sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of f and g on R\Z (Herglotz step A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both f(x) = π cot πx and g(x)=lim_{N→∞} Σ_{n=-N}^N 1/(x+n) are continuous for all non-integral x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For g show uniform convergence of the relevant series in a neighborhood of x (use comparison 1/(n^2 - x^2) < 1/(n-1)^2 for large n and the convergence of Σ 1/(n-1)^2). This justifies termwise manipulations and continuity claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodicity of f and g (Herglotz step B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both functions have period 1: f(x+1)=f(x) and g(x+1)=g(x) for x ∉ Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For f use cotangent's period π. For g use the truncated sums g_N(x) and the identity g_N(x+1)=g_{N-1}(x)+1/(x+N)+1/(x+N+1) and pass to the limit N→∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oddness of f and g (Herglotz step C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both f and g are odd functions: f(-x) = -f(x) and g(-x) = -g(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For f this is immediate from cotangent; for g observe g_N(-x) = - g_N(x) for the truncations and pass to the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common functional equation for f and g (Herglotz step D)
rubrics_metrics.description: f(x/2)+f((x+1)/2) = 2 f(x), and the same identity holds for g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For f derive from trigonometric addition theorems. For g manipulate the symmetric truncated sums (use rearrangement 1/(x/2 + n)+1/((x+1)/2 + n) = 2(1/(x + 2n) + 1/(x + 2n +1)) and take limits). This shared relation is crucial for the Herglotz argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous extension of h=f−g to integers with zeros (Herglotz step E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define h(x)=f(x)-g(x). By computing limits at integers one shows lim_{x→n} h(x)=0, so defining h(n):=0 yields a continuous function on all R sharing (B),(C),(D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Taylor series of sine/cosine or l'Hôpital's rule twice to show π cot πx - 1/x → 0 as x→0 (hence at all integers by periodicity), and check the remaining series tends to 0 as x→0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum/iteration argument to conclude h≡0 (Herglotz finale)
rubrics_metrics.description: If h is continuous, periodic, odd, and satisfies the functional equation, then its maximum m must be zero; iteration of the functional equation on a maximizer forces contradictions unless m=0, hence h(x)=0 for all x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick x0 with h(x0)=m. From the functional equation h(x0/2)+h((x0+1)/2)=m, iterate to obtain h(x0/2^n)=m and by continuity deduce h(0)=m, but h(0)=0, so m=0. Use oddness to rule out negative values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of ζ(2k) from y cot y expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: From y cot y = 1 - 2 Σ_{n=1}^∞ y^2/(π^2 n^2 - y^2) expand as a power series in y and identify coefficients to get ζ(2k) = Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n^{2k} expressed in terms of Bernoulli numbers and π^{2k}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite denominators via geometric series in y^2/(π^2 n^2), interchange sums, compare coefficients of y^{2k}. This yields ζ(2k) = (−1)^{k−1} 2^{2k−1} B_{2k} π^{−2k}/(2k)! (formula (9)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bernoulli numbers via z/(e^z − 1) expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Define B_n by z/(e^z − 1) = Σ_{n≥0} B_n z^n/n!. From parity and analyticity deduce B_n=0 for odd n≥3 and B_1 = −1/2; recursion follows from comparing (e^z − 1)(Σ B_n z^n/n!) = z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coefficient comparison to obtain recursive relations (equation (8)) that allow computation of Bernoulli numbers; these numbers feed into the ζ(2k) formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'short needle' (Buffon)
rubrics_metrics.description: A needle of length ℓ is 'short' relative to line spacing d if ℓ ≤ d (so it cannot cross two lines simultaneously, events of touching have probability zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction simplifies the problem because probabilities of multiple crossings vanish and the desired crossing-probability equals the expected number of crossings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulation: for short needle p = expected number of crossings
rubrics_metrics.description: For a short needle the probability p that it crosses a line equals the expected number E of crossings, because p2,p3,...=0 and E = p1 + 2p2 + ... reduces to E = p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation allows use of linearity of expectation and functional equations for E to compute p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity and homogeneity of expected crossings E(ℓ)
rubrics_metrics.description: E(x + y) = E(x) + E(y); by induction and scaling E(r x) = r E(x) for rational r, and monotonicity in x≥0 implies E(x) = c x for some constant c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The additivity comes from linearity of expectation and splitting the needle into segments; monotonicity and density of rationals extend linearity to all real x≥0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of constant c via Barbier's circle argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Drop a circular 'needle' C of diameter d (length x = d π) which always produces exactly two intersections, approximate C by inscribed/circumscribed polygons and use E(length)=c·length to deduce c d π = 2, hence c = 2/(d π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate circle by polygons P_n (inscribed) and P^n (circumscribed), compare expected intersections E(P_n) ≤ E(C) ≤ E(P^n), let n→∞ to get c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral/orientation averaging method for Buffon's needle
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability p can be computed by averaging over needle orientations α: p = (2/π) ∫_{0}^{π/2} (ℓ sin α)/d dα for short needles, yielding p = (2/π)(ℓ/d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the needle's orientation uniformly in [0,π/2] (account for symmetry), compute vertical projection ℓ sin α and the crossing event probability as min(1, (ℓ sin α)/d) for long needles handle piecewise cases where ℓ sin α > d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeon-hole principle (basic and strengthened form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n objects are placed in r boxes (r < n) at least one box contains >1 object. Strengthened: there exists a box a with |f^{-1}(a)| ≥ ceil(n/r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for existence proofs; represent mappings between finite sets and apply counting bounds. Many combinatorial existence results follow immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: two numbers with one dividing the other in any n+1 subset of {1,...,2n}
rubrics_metrics.description: From any A ⊆ {1,...,2n} with |A| = n+1 there are always two numbers in A such that one divides the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write each a ∈ A as 2^k m with odd m; there are only n possible odd parts between 1 and 2n−1, so by pigeonhole two numbers share the same odd part and hence one divides the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequence theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: In any sequence of mn+1 distinct real numbers there exists an increasing subsequence of length m+1 or a decreasing subsequence of length n+1 (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate to each element ai the length t_i of the longest increasing subsequence starting at ai. If all t_i ≤ m, pigeonhole on t_i-values gives >n indices with same t and forces a decreasing subsequence of length n+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of monotone subsequences to bound permutation-dimension dim(Kn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated application of the monotone subsequence theorem to representing permutations yields lower bounds such as dim(Kn) ≥ log2 log2 n (via iterative extraction of long monotone subsequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the theorem p times to nested subsequences to eventually obtain a 3-tuple monotone in all permutations, yielding contradictions unless sufficient permutations are used; this produces the logarithmic-logarithmic lower bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefix-sum modulo trick for consecutive subsequence sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n integers a1,...,an, there exists a consecutive block whose sum is multiple of n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider prefix sums s_m = a1+...+am mod n for m=0..n. There are n+1 sums but only n residues, so two equal residues give a consecutive block whose difference is 0 mod n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double counting / incidence counting principle
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite sets R and C and S ⊆ R×C, summing incident counts by rows equals summing by columns: Σ_{p∈R} r_p = |S| = Σ_{q∈C} c_q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model with incidence matrix A (entries 0/1); counting by rows or columns yields the same total. This is a fundamental tool for deriving average or global combinatorial bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average number of divisors via double counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Average t̄(n) = (1/n) Σ_{j=1}^n t(j) satisfies H_n − 1 < t̄(n) < H_n, hence log n − 1 < t̄(n) < log n + 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count the 1's in incidence matrix of 'i divides j' by rows (multiples of i up to n gives floor(n/i)) and columns (t(j)). Use harmonic number bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of degrees identity in graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: For graph G=(V,E), Σ_{v∈V} d(v) = 2|E|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count incident vertex-edge pairs; each edge contributes two to the total. This identity is a starting point for many graph theoretic estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double counting + Cauchy–Schwarz for extremal graphs (no C4) — Reiman bound
rubrics_metrics.description: If graph G on n vertices contains no 4-cycles, count pairs (u,{v,w}) where u adjacent to both v and w, bound common neighbors ≤1, apply Cauchy–Schwarz to degrees to derive |E| ≤ (n/4)(1 + √(4n − 3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute Σ_u (d(u) choose 2) ≤ (n choose 2) and manipulate with Cauchy–Schwarz and degree-sum identity to obtain a quadratic in |E| whose solution yields the bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-geometry construction (projective plane graph G_p) to nearly achieve Reiman bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct G_p whose vertices are 1-dimensional subspaces of (Z_p)^3, join [v] and [w] if their dot product is zero; this graph has n = p^2 + p + 1 vertices and edge count nearly reaching the Reiman bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count vertices and degrees via linear algebra: each vertex has degree p or p+1 depending on lying on the conic x^2+y^2+z^2=0. Use adjacency matrix A with A^2 = p I + J to compute eigenvalues and trace, which yields counts of degree-p vertices (trace A = p+1) and hence exact |E|.
